newsitem.title: USA: No apology to Nancy Reagan on Clinton TV ad.
newsitem.headline: No apology to Nancy Reagan on Clinton TV ad.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's campaign manager wrote Nancy Reagan on Wednesday, saying a commercial that shows an assassination attempt on her husband was scheduled to stop running soon but not apologising for it.

Separately, Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart told reporters the president had written a personal letter to Mrs. Reagan about the use of footage of the attack on former President Ronald Reagan. Lockhart said that letter would not be made public.

Nancy Reagan wrote Clinton earlier this week to object to the television advertisement, which features former Reagan press secretary Jim Brady. Brady was badly injured in the March 1981 assassination attempt outside a Washington hotel.

The letter from Clinton/Gore campaign manager Peter Knight, released to reporters returning to Washington after a four-day campaign trip with Clinton, said the ad would stop running on Thursday, as scheduled, but did not offer an apology to Mrs. Reagan or promise not to use the footage again.

Knight's letter said the ad was prepared with the approval of Brady and his wife, Sarah, crusaders for gun control. It added that if the campaign took up the issue again, it would weigh Mrs. Reagan's views.
"Our intention was to express their (the Bradys') strongly held views about gun control and to highlight President Clinton's commitment to reducing crime and making our streets safer," Knight said.
"Should we choose to continue to run a commercial highlighting the Brady Bill issue, you can be assured we will take your views into consideration," the letter added.
The Brady bill, which imposes a mandatory five-day waiting period for handgun purchases, so background checks can be made on people seeking to buy the weapons, was signed into law by Clinton.
Earlier, White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters that the ad that Mrs. Reagan had objected to "was due to run its course in the next day or so."
Information on where, when and how often the commercial had been used was not immediately available from the campaign.

Another Clinton commercial was the target of criticism earlier this week. In it, Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter, Polly, was kidnapped and killed in California several years ago, credited Clinton with courage for pushing a tough anti-crime bill.
Clinton leads his Republican opponent, Bob Dole, by a wide margin with only two weeks until the Nov. 5 election.
